hints: If the rain looks vertical when he walks at 3 km/h, what is the rain’s own horizontal component? Then use the second observation for the vertical one.
worded:
1. Rain appears vertical at 3 km/h, so the rain’s horizontal component equals his speed: 3 km/h, in his direction of walking.

2. At 6 km/h, the apparent horizontal part is 3 − 6 = −3 km/h (towards him), and the vertical part is the rain’s own v_y.

3. 45° with the vertical means equal parts: v_y = 3 km/h.

4. Rain speed = √(3² + 3²) = 3√2 ≈ 4.24 km/h.
conventional:
![](asset:P000264-sol-1)

Let $\vec{v}_{R} = p\ihat  - q\jhat $ (x along his walk, y up).

(i) $\vec{v}_{R} - 3\ihat $ vertical $\Rightarrow p = 3$.

(ii) $\vec{v}_{R} - 6\ihat  = - 3\ihat  - q\jhat $ at $45^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow q = 3$.

$$\left| \vec{v}_{R} \right| = \sqrt{3^{2} + 3^{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}\unit{km/h}.$$
mistakes: The real rain is not vertical here: it has a horizontal part of 3 km/h.
3 km/h alone is only one component.

check.solved_answer: $3\sqrt{2}$ km/h (at 45° to the vertical, slanting forward).
